brief: I work on customer experience at Grüns (gruns.co). A subscriber emailed us: her July box sat in a hot mailbox for two days, the gummies in several daily packs fused into a lump, and she's asking whether they're still safe to eat and why she should keep paying for a subscription that 'can't survive summer.' Please write my email reply, under 180 words. For this exercise, assume our policy is: we reship a replacement box free, no return needed, and she can pause or move her next shipment date from her account page. Don't make health or safety claims we can't back; tell her not to eat product that looks or smells off and that we'd rather replace it. Warm, direct, no corporate filler.

I'm on the finance team at Grüns (gruns.co). Growth wants to test a 3-month prepaid plan at a deeper discount alongside our monthly subscription. Write a one-page decision memo for the leadership meeting: recommendation up front, the math, the risks, and what we'd need to see in a 60-day test to keep it. Use these hypothetical exercise figures, not company data: monthly plan price $79; product cost $15 per box; fulfillment and shipping $9 per box either way; monthly churn 9% in each of the first three months, then 6%; prepaid plan $199 upfront for three boxes (about 16% off); 30% of new subscribers expected to choose prepaid. Show contribution per customer over six months for each plan and state your assumption about renewal after the prepaid term.

I lead support at Linear (linear.app) and I'm hiring a Product Support Engineer who will answer questions from developers and product managers, reproduce bugs, write clear issue reports for engineering, and improve our help docs. Please write the job posting in Markdown: a short opening about the work, what you'll do in the first 90 days, what we're looking for, nice-to-haves, and how the interview process works (four steps, keep it simple). The role is remote across North American time zones. Keep it under 600 words, in a plain, confident voice with no clichés like 'rockstar' or 'fast-paced environment'. Leave salary as a placeholder [range] that I'll fill in.

I'm a product designer at Linear (linear.app). We're reworking the onboarding checklist a workspace admin sees in the sidebar during their first week. Write the copy for six checklist items: invite teammates, create your first team, import issues from Jira or GitHub, set up a cycle, connect GitHub so pull requests link to issues, and turn on Slack notifications. For each item give a title (max 5 words), a one-line description (max 14 words) and button text (max 3 words), plus one short line shown when everything is done. Tone: calm, precise, no exclamation marks, no emoji. Return it as a Markdown table.

I'm on the wholesale team at Allbirds (allbirds.com). Write a first-touch email to the owner of an independent running and walking shop in Portland, Oregon, whom I met briefly at a trade show last month. The goal is a 20-minute call about carrying a small selection of our everyday sneakers for spring. Keep it under 140 words, with a subject line and one alternate subject line. Use [Shop name] and [Owner first name] placeholders. Don't promise margins, exclusivity or specific products; say we can share a line sheet and terms on the call. Friendly, not salesy.

I run customer support operations at Allbirds (allbirds.com). I need an internal holiday-season support plan covering 15 November to 15 January, written for my team leads. Hypothetical exercise figures, not company data: normal volume is 1,800 tickets a week; we expect 2.5x at peak in the week after Black Friday and a second spike of 2x in the first week of January for returns and exchanges; 14 agents each handle about 140 tickets a week; we can add up to 8 seasonal agents, who need two weeks of training. Cover staffing by week, coverage hours, the top contact reasons to prepare macros for, an escalation path for lost or late parcels, the daily metrics we'll watch with thresholds, and what we do if the backlog passes 48 hours. Use tables where they help.

I'm an account executive at Ramp (ramp.com), selling to finance leaders at US companies with 100 to 500 employees that still run expenses through reimbursements and spreadsheets. Write a three-email outbound sequence to a VP of Finance, sent on day 1, day 4 and day 10. Each email under 120 words, with a subject line, one clear ask, and a different angle each time: month-end close time, chasing receipts, and controlling spend before it happens. Use [First name] and [Company] placeholders. Don't quote customer results, savings figures or prices; I'll add proof points myself. Plain language, no hype words.

I'm on the strategy and research team at Ramp (ramp.com). Write an analysis memo on why small-business customers go inactive in their first year and what to do about it. Use these hypothetical exercise figures, not company data: 2,000 small-business accounts opened in Q1; by month 12, 26% were inactive. The account team tagged each inactive account with one primary reason: low adoption, two or fewer cards issued (41%); never connected accounting software (23%); business closed or acquired (18%); moved spend to another provider (18%). Active accounts averaged 9 cards issued and 92% had accounting connected. Cover what the data does and doesn't tell us, three ranked hypotheses, an experiment to test each next quarter with success metrics, and what we should start measuring. About 1,000 to 1,400 words.

I lead brand marketing at Sweetgreen (sweetgreen.com). Write a one-page creative brief for our agency for a fall seasonal menu launch. Treat the menu as placeholder items: [warm bowl 1], [warm bowl 2], [seasonal salad]. Audience: weekday lunch customers in cities who order through our app and haven't ordered in 60 or more days. Channels: app push, email, Instagram and in-store signage. Include the objective, a single-minded message, reasons to believe (only ones I can verify, so leave placeholders where needed), mandatories, tone, a deliverables list and a three-week timeline. Hypothetical exercise target, not company data: win back 8% of the lapsed group within 30 days.

I'm a regional people partner at Sweetgreen (sweetgreen.com), hiring a restaurant general manager (Head Coach, in our terms) for a new location. Write a structured guide for the final 45-minute interview: eight questions covering team leadership, hiring and developing hourly team members, food safety, handling a lunch rush with two people out, recovering a guest's bad experience, and managing numbers like labor and food cost. For each question add what a strong answer includes, one red flag, and a 1-to-4 rating anchor. End with a short scoring summary table. Keep every question legal and job-related; nothing about age, family, health or immigration status.

I work on lifecycle at Duolingo (duolingo.com). Write 10 push notification options for learners who had a streak of 30 or more days and missed yesterday, so the streak is gone. Each needs a title of no more than 30 characters and a body of no more than 90 characters. Keep our playful voice, but nothing guilt-tripping or passive-aggressive, since these people just lost something they cared about. At least three should point them to a five-minute lesson today, and at least two should mention starting a new streak. Put them in a Markdown table with character counts for each title and body.

I'm a product manager on the learning team at Duolingo (duolingo.com). Write a decision memo on whether to ship an experiment that added an optional end-of-lesson recap screen showing the three words the learner missed most. Hypothetical exercise figures, not company data: 4-week test, 400,000 learners per arm; day-7 retention 54.1% control vs 54.6% test (p = 0.08); lessons per learner per week 11.2 control vs 10.7 test; 63% of learners skipped the recap; among learners who viewed it, accuracy on those words in the next session rose from 71% to 79%. Cover the result, how to read each metric, the trade-off between learning and engagement, the risks of shipping or not shipping, a recommendation, and a follow-up test. About 900 to 1,300 words, with a short summary at the top.
